transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Session begins. Each player has Petra 3 FP, Anselm 3 FP, Caddock 3 FP, Yarrow 3 FP. Face-up: Endless Rain [H-01], The Causeway Wardens [F-03].

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Rain hammers the plank roofs of Hollowmoot as you file toward the toll-gate at the market end of the stilt-town, where the Causeway Wardens have strung chains across the walkway and a queue of soaked refugees waits under guttering lanterns. Torches hiss against the downpour; a Warden sergeant with red-rimmed eyes checks names against a waterlogged ledger while two more stand the chain with hooks and burn-brands, watching every cough in the crowd like it might be the hive. Somewhere behind you the market stalls sell charms and dried fish under tarps, and somewhere ahead, past the chain, is whatever brought each of you to this crossing tonight. The Wardens are undermanned and frightened, and it shows — short tempers, quick chains, a fire already lit and waiting.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: I know you, Rell. I know what you're really looking for.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra steps out of the crowd and approaches Warden Sergeant Rell, her eyes carefully studying his patterns—which refugees he scrutinizes closely, which ones pass easily, where his fear truly lies beneath the official procedures. She watches the hooks, the fire, the way his fingers grip his ledger.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: Sergeant, I'm trained in the old exorcism rites. I know the marks the hive leaves that others miss—I can help you sift the truly sick from those just soaked and scared.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm steps forward from the crowd, moving with the quiet confidence of someone who has actually faced the thing that keeps these Wardens awake at night. He approaches Sergeant Rell directly, keeping his hands visible and his voice low and steady against the rain.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: Sergeant. I'm Caddock, the midwife. I've got work waiting on the other side of that chain, and neither of us has time for bureaucracy.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock strides through the queue toward Sergeant Rell, water streaming off her heavy cloak, moving with the unshakeable confidence of someone who has made life-or-death decisions in far worse weather. She doesn't wait her turn—she walks straight to the chain.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: Sergeant Rell—you're stretched thin and scared, and that's when mistakes happen. Let Brack do what he was born for. He'll know the hive-touched before they ever cough.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow pushes through the crowd toward the chain with Brack at his heel, movements deliberate and calm. He lets the hound range along the edge of the refugee queue—even in the downpour, Brack's scarred muzzle works methodically at the air, inhaling deep, tracking infection through flood and rain like he's done a hundred times before in the Sallowmere. Meanwhile, Yarrow's own eyes move across the waiting people, reading the subtle signs: tremor in the hands, that peculiar glassy stare, the way fever makes a person hunch. His experience shows.)

transcript.speaker: Table

transcript.text: Yarrow — create advantage with Notice: dice 0 0 - -, invoking Brack tracks scent through any flood [YA-02] → Great (+4) vs Fair (+2): SUCCESS

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Rell's ledger stops moving. Petra watches him flinch at the word 'looking'—she's read him true: he isn't hunting the hive-touched at all, he's terrified of what happens when Hollowmoot finds out how few chains they really have. Anselm's steady recitation of the old marks, spoken low and sure, settles something in the sergeant's shoulders; here, finally, is someone who won't waste his time guessing. Brack noses down the queue and comes up clean, tail low but certain, and Yarrow reads the same in the crowd's trembling hands — no sickness here, only cold and fear, and Rell's men ease their grips on the hooks. Caddock doesn't even have to raise her voice; she simply walks through the gap the others have opened, and Rell waves her past with the distracted nod of a man who has decided, in the space of one conversation, that these four aren't his problem tonight. The chain drops. Behind you Hollowmoot's lantern-lit market sprawls into the dark, tarps sagging under the endless rain, and whatever business brought each of you here is, at last, within reach.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: Vess, I remember those days at the toll-gate—you're right, I still owe you for that crossing. I'm good for it when things settle, but right now I need to know: what's the favor?

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Petra accepts the compel on 'A Stranded Ferryman'.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Vess doesn't lead you to Rell's lean-to after all — he glances at the sergeant's chained gate, then jerks his chin toward the black water lapping under the pilings. Down a rickety ladder, his punt sits half-swamped at its mooring, and he's bailing it with a dented pot, cursing under his breath. "Not here," he mutters, eyes flicking to the shadows between the stilts. "Owe the Wardens for the mooring fee, owe the Marrows for the pole, owe half the ferry-row for favors I can't remember taking. You want passage past the chains quiet-like? Help me get this boat seaworthy and gone before sunup, and I'll owe you instead of them." Rain drums on the punt's cracked hull, each new leak a reminder of just how many debts are catching up to him at once.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: Vess, the west pilings—see how the water runs faster there, how it pulls? That's your channel past their chains. Rain like this drowns the sound, and they won't see us slip through.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra kicks off her boots and peers into the black water churning around the stilts, her eyes tracing how the pilings slice through the current. The rain drums its endless rhythm, and in that sound—that press of water against wood—she feels something her fingers learned at the ferry-work: the water's own preference for flow. There. The west pilings create a channel where the current accelerates, and more importantly, where the Warden's chains overhead leave a blind angle, a route hidden in plain sight.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: What's Vess asking you to do, Petra?

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm notices Petra's departure and makes a quiet excuse to the sergeant—something about checking the mooring-chains or the water level. He slips away from the lantern-light into the darkness and descends the rickety ladder carefully, hand on the wet wood, picking his way between the stilts toward the sound of bailing and Vess's muttered curses. When he reaches the water's edge, he surveys the half-swamped punt and its cargo of debts, his eyes moving between the ferryman and his companion.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: I've patched wounds that wouldn't stop bleeding and brought babies into storms—this boat's nothing but broken wood and panic. We'll have it seaworthy before those Wardens even realize we're gone.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock descends the ladder without hesitation and wades into the black water beside Vess. She examines the hull with practiced hands, her fingers finding the worst leaks and weak seams. She commandeers tools without asking and sets to work, moving with the same grim efficiency she brings to deliveries in impossible conditions.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: They're split thin and scared—that sergeant's whole attention is turned inland, worrying about what's creeping into town, not watching what leaves. The rain's drowning their sound discipline. We'll have a window if we move when Rell shifts his eyes inland again.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow climbs down to join them under the platform, moving into the shadows between the stilts where he can watch both the dark water below and the torchlight filtering through the planks above. He traces the Wardens' patrol patterns, reading the gaps in their coverage the way he reads water-flow.)

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Between the four of you the punt goes from wreck to worthy in near silence. Caddock's hands find every weak seam and pack them tight before the leaks can spread, while overhead Yarrow tracks Rell's every restless turn — the sergeant's eyes stay fixed inland, chasing shadows that aren't there, and never once dip toward the water. Petra's read on the current proves true: the west pilings hide a blind channel right under the chains, fast-flowing and drowned in the rain's noise. Vess stares at the sealed hull, then at the clear black water, like a man who hasn't been this close to a clean escape in years. "That's... that's it, then," he breathes, bailing pot forgotten in his hand. He owes Petra now, properly, and he knows it — and so does she. Before dawn breaks and the toll-gate wakes fully to its business, the punt slides free between the pilings, past the Wardens' blind angle, and out into open water, nobody the wiser.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: Mireth sold out a girl showing the first marks of hive-touch—her skin rippling, her eyes not quite focused. I'd come to her inn trying to learn if there was any soul left beneath the infection, if the hive could even be reasoned with. When the Wardens came sniffing around, Mireth gave her up rather than lose her license. I promised Mireth that I wouldn't hold it against her, that I understood what hunger and fear make us do. I meant it then. I mean it now.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: I see you in there, Mireth. I remember what I promised you. Go—save yourself. The rest of you, move.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Anselm accepts the compel on 'A Weary Innkeeper'.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Beat: A weary innkeeper Anselm once trusted for dry shelter — a woman named Mireth, who kept a lean-to near the old mill road — has sold out her latest lodgers, a hollow-eyed hive-touched family she hid for coin, straight to the pack hunting them. They come howling out of the reeds at Gullet Ford, following her betrayal like a scent. attacks at Gullet Ford using hooked spears thrust from the reed banks, because A long groan rises up through the waterlogged stone beneath the ford, the old shrine warning it's about to fall, and the tremor shudders through the mud and drives the hive-touched out of their collapsing den, starving and desperate for the first warm bodies they find..

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: The punt scrapes gravel at Gullet Ford just as a groan rolls up through the waterlogged stone underfoot — the old shrine beneath the crossing shifting, cracking, warning everyone within earshot that it means to fall. Then the reeds erupt: hollow-eyed shapes, the same hive-touched family Mireth traded away for a dry license, burst from their collapsing den with hooked spears wrenched from broken fence-stakes, pain-blind and starving, driven straight at the first warm bodies they find. Anselm's promise to Mireth curdles in his mouth — he understands now exactly what her fear cost these people. Water churns black around the punt's hull as the family closes from both banks, and somewhere beneath the mud the shrine groans again, closer to giving way.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: The shrine's singing—I hear it in the water, in the stone, like Saint Orrin's bells tolling backward. The north anchor-stones still hold, but the southern face is fractured. That's where it fails first.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra's eyes go distant as her ears catch the rising wail beneath the churning water. This is the sound she knows from years of bell-work: stone at the breaking point. She traces the shrine's death-song through the groaning beneath the ford, reading the fractures like a bell-pattern, and shouts the safe path to her companions—pulling them toward the ground that will still hold when the ancient stones give way.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: I know these waters, I know these stones—I've swum over them since I was small enough to drown. The shrine falls east. There's a channel there. Go. Now.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm closes his eyes for a heartbeat, listening past the rain and spear-clang to the ancient stone groaning beneath the ford. He's swum these broken mill-roads all his life, felt how they collapse. When he opens his eyes, he points sharply toward the eastern bank where the shrine's voice cracks most ominously—recognizing in that sound the exact pattern of collapse, the direction the stone will fall, the channel that will open.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: Hold fast. I've faced worse than starving things in the dark.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock seizes the punt pole and steps forward with unshakeable calm, her body positioned between the attacking pack and her companions, ready to meet their hooked spears with solid wood and steady hands.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: North flank is stable—move through there now!

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Brack's warning cuts through the rain as the family bursts from the reeds with their hooked spears. Yarrow's eyes snap across the ford, reading water and ground like he reads every weathered waterway—marking which stones of the old shrine still hold true beneath the floodwater, where solid ground remains clear for the retreat.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: I hear my sister in that cry, but she's not here. These people are. I won't hesitate now.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Anselm refuses a compel.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: The shrine gives its last warning groan and starts to go — but by then it doesn't matter. Petra's reading of the death-song, Anselm's memory of these drowned mill-roads, and Yarrow's eye for the one strip of stone still holding true all point the same way, and the punt threads through the collapse like it was never in danger at all: north flank solid, east channel open, the party moving as one while the ford buckles behind them. Caddock plants herself between the reeds and her companions and meets the hive-touched family's rush with the pole itself, driving one attacker back bloodied and reeling — Mireth's betrayal has cost these people enough, and Caddock's steady hands make sure it doesn't cost them their lives too, though a hooked spear rakes her ribs before the pack breaks off, scattering into the reeds as the last archway of the shrine slumps into the water behind them. Anselm doesn't get the reckoning he came for — no words with the girl, no proof the hive leaves anything human behind — but he doesn't hesitate either, and that refusal costs him nothing but the ghost of his sister's voice, unanswered, in the rain. The punt scrapes clear onto solid ground on the far bank, soaked, shaken, gear intact, the shrine's grave sealed by broken stone.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: I promised Fennick coin from the Blackwater Cartel for helping a pregnant woman—one of the survivors from the burning of Marrowreed—slip past Rell's checkpoint without drawing attention. The reward hasn't come through because I haven't been able to reach my contact to authorize the payment yet, and everything's been chaos since the shrine at Gullet Ford came down.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: This is earnest money, Fennick. The rest comes at dawn when I reach my contact. Sell me out and the Cartel will make damn sure you regret it.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Caddock accepts the compel on 'Promise of Reward'.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Beat: The runner who stumbles up the ford-path isn't a Warden at all — it's Fennick, the ledger-boy Caddock once promised coin for help getting his family out of Marrowreed. He's soaked through, out of breath, and clutching a strip of oilcloth with names scrawled on it. arrives with word that Every toll-debt written in ledgers up and down the Causeway has been called in at once — the Wardens, desperate for coin and hands, are collecting on every favor and unpaid crossing tonight, all together. has happened.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Fennick half-collapses against a fallen shrine-stone, oilcloth clutched to his chest like it might dissolve in the rain. "Every ledger, Caddock — every debt, every crossing owed, called in tonight. Rell's got the list. Your name's on it twice." He thrusts the strip of cloth out: names, tally-marks, a column with Caddock's own scrawled promise circled in charcoal. Behind him, torchlight bobs along the causeway — Wardens moving house to house, gate to gate, collecting. The ford, the punt, the road north — nothing crosses free tonight, and Fennick still hasn't been paid for what he already did.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: Show me that—whose names are marked? Is mine there?

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra reaches for the oilcloth strip, pulling it close to read the familiar tally-marks and scripted names of the Causeway ledgers. She's lived in these debt-marks her whole life; somewhere on that list is her own name, marked with back-taxes she can't pay. But that's secondary now—what matters is figuring out which debts Rell will hunt first and how fast those torches are moving.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: Caddock keeps his promises. Fennick will have his coin.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm steps forward between the approaching torchlight and his companions, a hand settling on Fennick's shoulder. His voice carries the same steady certainty he showed at the toll-gate—not a negotiation, just a statement of fact.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: Get to cover, Fennick. I'm going to Wick Lane to settle this with the Cartel before those Wardens reach us. I deliver on my promises.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock grabs the oilcloth from Fennick's hands and reads her name circled in charcoal with a bitter snarl. She shoves it back at him, then immediately moves toward the water's edge. She uses the burned ground and the waterlogged channels around Gullet Ford—paths she's learned by heart—to slip past the Warden patrols moving house to house. She moves fast and direct, not bothering with stealth so much as sheer capability: she knows these flooded roads better than Rell's soldiers ever will.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: The rain's our ally here—it drowns sound and covers movement. I know the water-routes better than any Warden; we can slip past them in the dark if we move now.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow crouches in the shrine's shadow, watching the torchlight bob along the causeway while rain hammers down. His eyes trace the Wardens' positions—reading gaps and patterns the way he once read flood-lines. He knows where they're thin, where the marsh offers passage that embankment-bound guards will never think to watch.)

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Caddock doesn't so much sneak as *stride* — she knows every scar of burned ground around Gullet Ford, every channel the fire left behind, and she cuts through the Wardens' sweep like the checkpoint was never there, oilcloth debt-list forgotten at her back. Behind her, Yarrow reads the torchlight the way he reads flood-lines, marking where the patrols thin and where the reeds swallow sound — he calls the gaps low and sure, and the whole party finds the marsh opening up ahead of them, a route through the water that no embankment-bound Warden will ever think to watch. Rain drowns their footsteps; the ledger-boy's news, so dire a moment ago, curdles into just noise behind them. By the time Rell's torches converge on the ford-path, there's nothing there but wet stone and a groaning, half-collapsed shrine. Fennick, still unpaid, still scared, melts into the dark with Anselm's promise ringing in his ears.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: Elara, my sister. She drowned in the first great swell when the weirs were failing—I was with her at the north gate, trying to shore it up. I was too slow reaching her when the water came. I swore then that I would see her properly buried, in the old way, with her name spoken aloud.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: The names have to be spoken—that's the covenant. Elara's name will be heard, no matter what else comes.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Yarrow accepts the compel on 'Duty to the Dead'.

transcript.speaker: Table

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: The path bends and opens onto the sunken burial-ground, half-drowned headstones poking from black water like broken teeth, and Yarrow is already there ahead of the others, mid-vigil, one hand on a marker he's cleared of silt. Torchlight swims through the rain from up the path — not Wardens this time, but a procession: two acolytes of the Drowned Priest at its head, chanting the swarm-hymn low, and behind them a mob of Hollowmoot's own, tavern-drunk on gossip and fear, carrying planks and rope like they mean to drag the dead up and out. One acolyte raises a hand toward the water and calls out that the bodies belong to the hive now, that drowning was a mercy and a claiming, and the crowd surges a step closer to where Yarrow stands between them and the graves. Elara's marker is close enough that Yarrow could touch it without moving.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: The swarm-song rejects them. These graves are already spoken for—the hive wants no part of names already claimed by the dead themselves.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra cuts into the procession's path, hand raised as if listening to something only she perceives. She invokes "Hears the swarm-song before others do" from PE-03, drawing on her deep attunement to the collective voice beneath Hollowmoot. The truth rings clear: the living acolytes are speaking lies into a song that knows better.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: These graves answer to older bonds than the hive's reach. The dead here are not yours to claim.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm steps forward, placing himself as a physical barrier between Yarrow and the advancing crowd. He speaks in the low, certain cadence of old exorcism rites—words that mark and protect burial ground, that bind the dead to their rest. His voice carries the weight of knowledge that predates the swarm-song, absolute and immovable.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: You want these bodies? You'll have to come through me. I've stood in worse weather and worse odds. Try it.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock strides forward and plants herself squarely between the advancing mob and the graves, filling the narrow path with the solid certainty of someone who has survived worse than a crowd of half-drunk townspeople. Her shoulders set, her hands spread—the same hands that have brought dozens of children into the world are now making it clear that these dead will not be disturbed.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: I stood at the north gate when the water came and took my sister. I was too slow reaching her—that's a weight I'll carry forever. But I won't fail the dead now. You will not disturb these graves. Not while I draw breath.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow steps forward until he stands directly in front of Elara's burial marker, positioning himself as an immovable barrier. His posture straightens—feet planted wide, shoulders back, one hand settling on his knife hilt. There's the stance of someone who has held gates during floods, who has stood watch through worse than tavern-drunk mobs. Every line of his body says: you cannot pass this line.)

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: The mob's charge breaks against four bodies planted like pilings. Petra's cry rings out over the chanting — the swarm-song rejects false priests — and something in the acolytes' own hymn seems to falter, the crowd behind them faltering with it, torches guttering as doubt spreads faster than rain. Anselm's old rite settles over the graves like a lid closing; whatever claim the Drowned Priest meant to lay here simply doesn't take, the words sliding off consecrated ground that predates any swarm. Voss's shrieked barb — that the swarm claims all who reach too slow, a blade aimed straight at Yarrow's oldest wound — breaks on Yarrow's stance instead of his resolve; he doesn't so much as blink, one hand still resting on Elara's marker. And when the front line of drunk, torch-lit townsfolk finally surges as one, planks and rope swinging for the graves, it's Caddock who eats the charge and gives nothing back, and Yarrow's blade turning the last of them from the stone — the mob buckles, stumbling backward into the mud, torches hissing out in the downpour one by one until the procession is just two acolytes and a scattering, shame-faced crowd melting into the dark. Voss spits a curse about the belltower's patience and retreats with what's left of them. Yarrow kneels at Elara's marker, rain running down his face, and speaks her name aloud — clear, unhurried, the covenant kept.

costs.text: A soaked ferryman corners Petra as she passes—he recognizes her from the tollgate days, says she still owes him for a crossing years back, and won't let her by until she settles up or does him a favor right now, in front of everyone.

Vess doesn't lead you to Rell's lean-to after all — he glances at the sergeant's chained gate, then jerks his chin toward the black water lapping under the pilings. Down a rickety ladder, his punt sits half-swamped at its mooring, and he's bailing it with a dented pot, cursing under his breath. "Not

A weary innkeeper Anselm once trusted for dry shelter — a woman named Mireth, who kept a lean-to near the old mill road — has sold out her latest lodgers, a hollow-eyed hive-touched family she hid for coin, straight to the pack hunting them. They come howling out of the reeds at Gullet Ford, followi

A long groan rises up through the waterlogged stone beneath the ford, the old shrine warning it's about to fall, and the tremor shudders through the mud and drives the hive-touched out of their collapsing den, starving and desperate for the first warm bodies they find.

Mireth recognizes Anselm in the chaos and, true to how she Sells Out Lodgers to save her own skin, shrieks to the pack exactly where he's standing — she's traded a lodger for her life before, and she does it again now, throwing him to the front of the attack to buy her own escape.

costs.tag: Haunted by his little sister's drowning cry
costs.text: As the shrine groans and the water churns black around the punt, the panicked shriek of a hive-touched child in the family snags something raw in Anselm — for one frozen heartbeat he hears his sister's drowning cry instead, and hesitates exactly when he can least afford to.

The runner who stumbles up the ford-path isn't a Warden at all — it's Fennick, the ledger-boy Caddock once promised coin for help getting his family out of Marrowreed. He's soaked through, out of breath, and clutching a strip of oilcloth with names scrawled on it.

Every toll-debt written in ledgers up and down the Causeway has been called in at once — the Wardens, desperate for coin and hands, are collecting on every favor and unpaid crossing tonight, all together.

Fennick grabs Caddock's sleeve, words tumbling out fast: "You said there'd be coin, that's the only reason I came out in this rain — so pay it now, tonight, or the reward never materialises for me, and I'll sell where you're hiding to the first debt-collector who'll listen."
The path bends toward the sunken burial-ground, where Yarrow keeps vigil — he guards the drowned bodies there, unwilling to let the flood claim their names along with their lives.

As the acolytes and their tavern-mob bear down on the burial-ground, Yarrow refuses to move until he finishes reading the names of the dead aloud — the delay lets the Drowned Priest's people reach the goal first and claim it in front of the gathered crowd.

ambiguities.issue: §6.4 says an Altered-scene draw's tags 'change one element of the planned scene' (flavor only), while §4's enumerated draw triggers do not list Altered scenes among the reasons for running the full 'Resolving a drawn player card' procedure (offer compel, surface card, grant free invoke). At event 21-24, the GM ran the full §4 resolution (compel on the weakness tag, card surfaced with a free invoke) on top of using a power tag to reframe the scene location, i.e. two different tags from one Altered-scene draw were used for two different effects.
ambiguities.interim_ruling: Table treated any Session Deck draw of a player card, regardless of which trigger caused it, as running the full §4 player-card resolution (compel + surface + free invoke) in addition to whatever the triggering rule (here §6.4) asked the draw to do.

ambiguities.section: §7 scene loop vs Beat Frame prep-triggers
ambiguities.issue: §7 step 1 says 'Run the scene test... except in the session's first scene,' with no exception written for a scene whose Beat Frame was already pre-triggered by an ordinary §7 trigger (as opposed to the explicit backstory-guarantee override in §4). Scene 3 opened directly with Beat Frame AMBUSH (trigger B-01 fired at scene 2 cleanup) with no scene_test event logged.
ambiguities.interim_ruling: The table skipped the scene test for scene 3 because a Beat Frame had already been pre-triggered at the previous cleanup, treating that as functionally equivalent to the guarantee-pull override even though the text only grants that override to the backstory guarantee.

ambiguities.issue: §3 states a player's own tags are live to them when the card is in their binder, and separately that 'anyone' may invoke a face-up rail tag. It does not say whether the GM/an opponent may directly invoke a player's live binder tag (weakness or otherwise) when that specific card is not face-up on the rail. At event 110 the GM hostile-invoked Petra's weakness tag PE-03 for 1 fate point even though PE-03 never appears in a rail_add event this session.
ambiguities.interim_ruling: The table allowed the GM to invoke a player's live (non-Strained) binder tag directly, paying 1 fate point, even though the card was never surfaced onto the rail, triggering the normal hostile-invoke fate-point payout to the target at scene end.

friction.text: Multiple deck-draw costs/compels initially failed the 'the cost must use the tag' rule (§3) and were flagged repaired=true (H-06's WHY fill, and the PX-03, PX-17 and PX-22 compels), showing this constraint is being missed on the first pass fairly often and needs GM rework mid-scene.

The same top card (C-03) was peeked by three different players in a row (events 57, 59, 61) within one scene, each time left on top with no new information gained — the success-with-style peek option produces repetitive, low-value moments when several players roll SWS against the same drawn hazard in sequence.

It's unclear from the rail/free-invoke rules whether the free invokes granted on module cards C-04 and F-01 (events 93-94) were ever actually spent in scene 5; nothing in the log shows them used before scene end, leaving GMs to guess whether unused module free invokes were simply wasted by design.

free_text.best_moment: The shrine's death-song at Gullet Ford. Petra's entire concept is "hears the swarm-song before others do," and actually *reading the stone's voice* to navigate the party through a collapsing shrine—and pulling it off with style—felt like the perfect mechanical payoff to what she fundamentally is. The Notice roll mattered because only she could read that particular language.
free_text.most_frustrating: I stayed at 5 fate points the whole session and never got to really hoard and leverage my advantage. Most of my rolls were creating advantages for the group or supporting others' mechanical moments (Caddock's Physique, Anselm's Lore, Yarrow's Notice). I wanted a climactic scene where Petra herself was under direct pressure and had to *spend* to win something she personally needed, not just read something correctly for the party.
free_text.background_used: Yes, extensively: Ashwater Tollgate debt, Vess's ferry-debt, her intimate knowledge of water-flow and weather-reading, the swarm-song at her core, bell-patterns, all used naturally. How it landed: Good. None of it felt like box-checking—her background genuinely shaped what she could contribute and why she mattered to the story.
free_text.wanted_but_couldnt: I wanted Petra to face a direct personal conflict where she had to fight for something *she* wanted, not just contribute expertise to the group's survival. A moment where her Notice wasn't enough and she had to invoke and spend and risk, rather than just read the situation correctly.
free_text.one_sentence: Petra's background—the bell-work, the swamp-sense, the debt history, the swarm-song attunement—was woven into the actual story beats rather than just character flavor, and it felt like central to why she mattered.

free_text.best_moment: Gullet Ford—when Anselm recognized the mill-roads' collapse pattern and guided the party to safety while refusing to be paralyzed by his sister's drowning. It was overcoming his central wound by doing what he actually excels at, not being frozen by grief.
free_text.most_frustrating: Couldn't get dialogue with the hive-touched girl; that was my main entry point for the scene and the shrine collapse/combat prevented any real confrontation about whether she retained her humanity. That's the core question driving Anselm.
free_text.background_used: The Mireth compel landed excellent—it embodied Anselm's central moral uncertainty perfectly. The mill-roads knowledge and exorcism rites were also well-earned. Everything felt good.
free_text.wanted_but_couldnt: Get dialogue with the hive-touched girl and hear whether the infection preserves anything human. That's Anselm's driving question and I came to that scene hoping to get answers.
free_text.one_sentence: Used well—the Mireth compel especially cut right to my character's core uncertainty, and all the background integration felt earned rather than forced.

free_text.best_moment: Standing between the mob and Elara's grave. It's the purest expression of who Caddock is—unshakeable, protective, willing to meet force with force when the stakes demand it. The moment brings together her steady hands, her willingness to escalate, and a cause that matters beyond herself. Everything about that scene *is* Caddock.
free_text.most_frustrating: Nothing serious, but I wanted to actually reach Wick Lane and confront the Cartel contact instead of the session ending as I'm en route. That thread feels unresolved, though it's a natural stopping point for the session.
free_text.background_used: Extensively and beautifully. The GM pulled from every card—Marrowreed burning (the burned-ground knowledge, Fennick's debt), the hive-touched bond (why they didn't savage her at Gullet Ford), Wick Lane/Cartel (immediate stakes with the debt-list), her reputation as a midwife (confidence at the toll-gate). Each element created meaningful complications and reasons to act. This landed as excellent—nothing felt forced or unearned.
free_text.wanted_but_couldnt: Reach Wick Lane and actually face off with the Cartel contact. Also didn't get challenged on the "Cannot admit fault" weakness in a way that created real tension—there were opportunities, but they didn't come up naturally in this session. Neither is a real complaint; both feel like future session material.
free_text.one_sentence: Caddock's backstory was woven through every scene—it created stakes, complications, and reasons to act, and never once felt ignored or used unfairly.

free_text.best_moment: Standing at Elara's grave and speaking her name into the rain—the covenant kept. It was the culmination of everything Yarrow needed: a promise made good, his sister honored, his stance unmoved by both hive-lies and tavern-drunk mobs. The moment felt earned, personal, and mine.
free_text.most_frustrating: Not much, honestly. If anything: the session's pacing left no room to follow the flood upriver toward its true source, which is the driving thread of his whole REACH card. But that's more a wish for what comes next than a real frustration—immediate survival took priority, and that felt right.
free_text.background_used: Extensively. Elara's drowning, his water-reading, Brack's tracking, family maps, his weir-keeper knowledge—all of it wove through scenes naturally. The GM used his personal tragedy (sister's death, failed gate-keeping) as the heart of the burial-ground compel, and it landed perfectly: it tested him, gave him a real choice to refuse or accept, and let him resolve it through direct action. Felt organic, not forced.
free_text.wanted_but_couldnt: Investigate deeper into what's actually causing the flood—trace it upriver, use his obsession with the source-mystery to drive toward new discoveries. The session was packed with immediate threats and survival, which made sense tactically, but left no room for that slower, deliberate probe into his core question.
free_text.one_sentence: My backstory was central to nearly every major scene and felt earned rather than inflicted—especially the burial-ground defense, which gave Yarrow exactly the kind of personal, high-stakes moment his character needed.

chronicle.summary: In the flooded shadow of Saint Orrin's burial-ground, four wanderers stood between the Drowned Priest's acolytes and a graveyard the flood had not yet claimed, and won. Petra's ear for the swarm-song exposed Voss's lies, Anselm's old rites sealed the ground against the hive's claim, and Caddock and Yarrow broke the mob's charge with sheer immovable resolve. Yarrow knelt at last beside his sister Elara's marker and spoke her name aloud, the covenant kept, as the shame-faced procession dissolved into the rain.
